summary: Redwood AE+SE ran an edge-cases demo focusing on long-context handling, high TPS, and streaming backpressure/timeouts. Customer (MaplePay) is evaluating Dedicated vs Private deployment for latency-sensitive payments use case. Key concerns: tail latency under bursty TPS, streaming backpressure causing timeouts, KV cache behavior with 100k tokens prefix, and compliance (SOC2/KMS). Agreed next steps: share benchmarks, pricing, and schedule pilot.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-10-07
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Ana Morales (Redwood AE), David Chen (Redwood SE), Jared Liu (CTO, MaplePay), Priya Singh (Sr ML Eng), Lena Roberts (Infra)
Shared: demo deck (link), benchmark spreadsheet (link to google sheet), quickstart repo (link)

[00:00] Ana: Hi everyone, thanks for making time. i'm ana from Redwood, AE on the account. quick intros?
[00:08] Jared: Jared here, CTO at MaplePay. Priya and lena are with me.
[00:12] Priya: hey all, priya — i'll be driving the benchmark and integration.
[00:16] Lena: lena, infra focused, mainly networking and security.
[00:20] Ana: awesome. david from our infra team will run through the edge cases—long context, high TPS and streaming backpressure. david over to you.
[00:28] David: thanks ana. real quick agenda: 1) show API + console for long context, 2) demo high TPS using our stress harness, 3) demonstrate streaming and backpressure behavior and what happens when clients time out, 4) go over Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs.
[00:42] David: first, long context. we'll load a 100k token prefix, simulate a large KV cache and show how the runtime manages KV eviction and kernel selection. note, in this demo we use a quantized variant to keep throughput sane.
[01:05] Priya: quick q, how does the KV prefix caching work when you have many concurrent streams? do you shard the cache per worker?
[01:12] David: good question. we shard the KV caches by model shard and by worker instance, so concurrent requests benefit from local cache hits when affinity is preserved. however, with many unique prefixes you will see increased miss rates — that's where our prefix cache warmers and prefetch come in.
[01:28] Jared: any observed tail latency with 100k prefixes? when we tried locally we hit some 2.5s tails on token 1 for big prefixes.
[01:36] David: tail depends on seq len and kernel selection; typically cold starts can spike. in our configs on Dedicated we get p99s under 700-900ms for similar workloads, but on hosted tier you might see higher. also hinted that batching tradeoffs — if you want strict p99 you should pin to Dedicated and tune batch windows.
[01:54] Priya: are there any automatic fallbacks if a worker can't serve the long context? like a shorter window or partial KV?
[02:00] David: yes, our smart routing can fallback to compatible model variants or smaller context variants; you can set policy for graceful degrade vs fail-fast.
[02:08] Ana: quick aside on cost — long context is token-heavy; our Optimize toolkit will recommend quant + batch config to reduce per-token cost. we'll share an example later.

[02:20] David: moving to high TPS. we run a stress harness that can ramp from 100 tps to 2k tps across tenants. for the demo i'll show a 1k TPS burst and we can observe latency and backpressure.
[02:34] (demo starts, a short pause while David pulls up the harness)
[02:45] David: starting ramp now — you should see concurrent streams, and metrics in the console: per-route latency, token throughput, and queue depth.
[03:00] (console metrics spike)
[03:08] Priya: i'm seeing token emisson counts are high — small nit: emission spelled emisson in console (laughter).
[03:12] David: yeah sorry little typo in the debug UI, will fix. so as TPS increases we apply continuous batching; you'll see latency tradeoffs. we also have burst capacity to handle short spikes without scaling.
[03:28] Lena: is burst capacity on Dedicated only? we can't allow suddent cross-tenant noisy neighbor behavior in our VPC.
[03:34] Ana: good question — Dedicated provides isolated GPU pools with limits; Private can be deployed in your VPC for full isolation. burst capacity for Dedicated is configurable per-pool and limited by your reserved commit.

[03:48] David: now i want to demonstrate streaming backpressure. we're using chunked responses over SSE and we'll simulate a slow client that applies backpressure by reading slowly, and also a client that times out after 10s.
[04:02] (demo: simulated slow client)
[04:10] David: when a slow client causes buffer pressure the runtime prioritizes in-flight tokens and applies backpressure heuristics — that can cause upstream request queuing or drop to a fallback path if timeout thresholds are exceeded.
[04:24] Jared: what happens to billing if you drop a stream mid-generation? we can't have users billed for partial output they didn't get.
[04:30] Ana: we have consumption accounting that prorates on tokens successfully emitted and have retry semantics; our SDK exposes a streaming ACK so you can confirm delivery. we'll share the exact billing rules.
[04:42] Priya: and timeouts — do you recommend client-side retry or server-side keepalive?
[04:48] David: client-side retries with idempotency keys are recommended. on the server side we have keepalive pings and an adjustable idle timeout so long-lived idle streams won't hang resources.

[05:01] Lena: any known issues with http proxies (corporate proxies) and chunked SSE? we saw some proxies buffer and break streaming.
[05:09] David: yes proxies that buffer chunked transfer can add significant delay; for Private deployments inside your network you can control proxies or use websocket-based streaming to avoid intermediate buffering. we'll note that as an infra consideration.

[05:22] David: demo note — streaming backpressure can push request queue depth up and cause worker scheduling to increase; if workers hit memory thresholds we evict oldest cached prefixes to free space — that's an eventual degradation path.
[05:36] Priya: what about timeouts during KV cache warm-up? if we warm up and a request times out, will you retry using a warmed worker?
[05:43] David: we usually retry to a warmed worker if available based on routing policy; for strict latency SLOs we recommend a warmed pool with pre-warmed KV caches.

[05:55] (brief pause, David pulls up console showing error traces)
[06:05] David: showing an example trace where a slow client produced backpressure, queue depth increased, and a few requests hit the 10s client timeout and aborted. in the trace you can see the retry loop and fallback to a smaller model variant. note some text in trace autocorrected 'kv cache' to 'kv cash' in the transcript, which is a minor transcription issue.

[06:24] Jared: are logs auditable for compliance? we need immutable audit logs for payments.
[06:30] Ana: yes, Private + Dedicated options support enriched audit logs, retention policies and can integrate with your KMS/HSM for key material. SOC2 is supported and we can share our compliance pack.

[06:44] Priya: on the topic of privacy — are ephemeral inputs persisted? we want a mode where inputs are never stored.
[06:50] Ana: we support no-persistence mode in Private deployments; for Hosted we offer configurable retention and redaction. we'll include details in the security doc.

[07:00] David: next, a short perf tradeoff — batch window sizing. looking at this workload, toggling batch windows from 5ms to 20ms reduces tokens/sec cost by ~18% but increases p99 by ~120ms. you can tune per-route in Optimize to pick a cost/latency point.
[07:22] Priya: can Optimize suggest quantization levels too? we've seen quality drop with aggressive 4-bit quant.
[07:28] Ana: yes Optimize runs model-quality checks against your eval sets and will recommend quant+mixing strategies: e.g., use 4-bit for assistant tokens but 8-bit for context tokens or keep logits in fp16. it's a heuristic but we've seen good results.

[07:41] Jared: around pilot — we want to run a dedicated pilot with our 3 typical workloads: payment auth (real-time), fraud reranking (batch), and customer chat (long context). what's a minimal pilot look like?
[07:52] Ana: minimal pilot is 1-week with a small Dedicated pool or Private eval cluster. we run your prompts through our harness, measure p50/p95/p99, and recommend tuning. david will provide a benchmark repro and we can schedule start dates.

[08:04] (demo continues; David shares benchmark sheet)
[08:12] David: here's the benchmark sheet — columns: route, payload size, avg seq len, concurrency, target TPS, observed p50/p95/p99, token cost estimate. we'll attach this to the follow-up email.
[08:24] Priya: can we run with our SSO/SAML test tenant for auth? we want to verify audit flows.
[08:30] Ana: yes, for Private or Dedicated with SSO integration we can add your SAML IdP. again, security doc will outline steps.

[08:42] Jared: any gotchas with KMS integration? we use an HSM-backed KMS and need envelope encryption.
[08:48] David: we integrate with customer-managed KMS via envelope encryption; in Private deployment you can route key operations to your HSM. there might be latencies on first key unwrap but it's usually small.

[08:58] Lena: latency targets — we need <350ms p99 for payment auth under 500 TPS. is that realistic?
[09:05] David: on Dedicated with tuned batch windows and warmed cache, we have seen p99s in that ballpark for ~400-600 TPS for short responses. for 100k-context it's harder — the context length is the dominating factor. we suggested caching frequent prefixes and using smaller context for token 0 to keep p99.

[09:24] Priya: regarding SDKs, any recommended patterns for streaming with backpressure handling?
[09:29] David: yes, we provide SDK helpers for chunked backpressure management including the streaming ACK I mentioned, client-side buffering heuristics, and server side keepalive. we'll share code snippets in the follow-up repo.

[09:42] Ana: ok let's go into a simulated timeout scenario where client times out at 8s, we retry with idempotency key and route to a warmed worker.
[09:51] (demo runs scenario)
[10:00] David: in this run you can see first attempt aborts at 8s, retry goes to warmed worker and completes with slightly higher cost. notice console logs show retry reason and that billing shows tokens emitted across attempts.
[10:15] Jared: can we coalesce logs by idempotency key to simplify billing reconciliation?
[10:20] Ana: yes we provide grouped-view in billing exports; we'll enable that in the pilot.

[10:30] (pause for questions)
[10:35] Priya: two quick technical items: 1) what kernel selection for long seqs — any specialized attention kernels? 2) is there an LRU for KV cache or tuned eviction policy?
[10:44] David: we use a combination: for long seqs we pick kernels optimized for linear attention for certain models and fall back to blocked attention for compatibility; eviction is size-aware LRU with priority given to pinned prefixes if you mark them.
[11:00] Priya: will there be an impact on model quality when mixing kernel types?
[11:05] David: slight differences in numerical precision can happen with quantization + alternative kernels but Optimize flags regressions and we do A/B rollouts to monitor quality.

[11:18] Jared: any examples of customers who ran similar workloads?
[11:22] Ana: fintech customer X ran payment auth with long-ish context and saw reduced per-transaction token cost after Optimize tuning; we can share anonymized numbers in the case study.

[11:32] (wrap-up)
[11:35] Ana: recap and next steps: 1) ana to send pricing and pilot terms, 2) david to send benchmark sheet and repro scripts, 3) priya to hand over prompt set and representative logs, 4) schedule pilot start for week of 2025-10-20.
[11:50] Jared: sounds good, thanks everyone.
[11:53] Anna: thanks — talk soon.

Note: transcription contains occasional errors and swapped words (e.g., 'kv cash', 'emisson'). References to external artifacts: demo deck (https://redwood.example/deck), benchmark sheet (https://docs.google.com/sheet/example), repo (https://github.com/redwood/repro).
